title: Sofa Trends 2026: 7 Styles UK Homes Are Buying Right Now
metaTitle: Sofa Trends 2026: 7 Styles UK Homes Are Buying Right Now
metaDescription: The 7 sofa trends shaping UK living rooms in 2026, from curved silhouettes and bouclé to modular layouts and velvet's comeback. Shop the trends at Sofora.
excerpt: Curved silhouettes, touchable textures and loungier profiles: these are the seven sofa styles defining UK living rooms in 2026, and how to bring each one home.
contentHtml:
If you are sofa shopping in 2026, you have probably noticed that living rooms look softer than they used to. Sharp corners are giving way to gentle arcs, flat grey fabrics have been replaced by weaves you want to touch, and the cool minimalism of the last decade has warmed into something far more inviting. These are the seven sofa styles UK shoppers are actually buying right now.

The common thread is comfort you can see. Softer curves, deeper colours, tactile fabrics and lower, loungier profiles all push in the same direction: away from stiff, showroom-formal seating and towards sofas that look like they want to be lived on. Here is what is trending, why it works, and how to bring each look into your own home.

1. Curved sofas: soft geometry takes over

The defining silhouette of 2026 is the curve. Serpentine backs, rounded arms and gently bowed fronts are appearing across three-seaters, two-seaters and corner sofas alike, softening rooms that used to be all straight lines and right angles. Curves do more than look good: a wraparound shape naturally draws people into conversation and helps zone open-plan spaces without the need for walls or screens.

Curved designs work best in textured fabrics that emphasise the shape. Our Arco curved corner sofa pairs a sweeping five-seat arc with ivory bouclé, while the Juno curved three-seater brings the same soft geometry to a compact 200cm width that suits smaller living rooms. If you love the look but not the commitment, a curved armchair such as the Elsie tub chair adds the shape in a smaller dose.

2. Bouclé grows up

Bouclé is not new, but in 2026 it has matured. The oversized, shaggy loops of a few years ago have tightened into neater, more structured weaves that keep the signature nubby texture while shrugging off everyday wear far better. It remains the fabric designers reach for when they want instant warmth and a quietly luxurious feel.

Choose bouclé for living rooms rather than the busiest family seating: the looped surface can catch on jewellery, zips and pet claws. In a calm sitting room or a grown-up snug, though, few fabrics photograph or feel as good. Cream, ivory and oat remain the most versatile shades, layering easily over wooden floors and neutral walls.

3. Jumbo cord goes mainstream

Corduroy's chunkier sibling has moved from retro curiosity to genuine staple. Jumbo cord's wide ribs give sofas a relaxed, tactile surface that hides creasing and everyday marks far better than flat weaves, which makes it a quietly practical choice for family homes. It also brings a soft seventies warmth that flatters both modern and traditional rooms.

Natural, oat and sage tones lead the way, keeping the look earthy rather than costume-y. The Dune low-profile corner sofa and the Reed three-seater both use the fabric to full effect, and because the ribs run vertically, the texture adds a subtle sense of height to lower designs.

4. Velvet's big comeback

Velvet is having a proper revival, and this time it is less about formal drawing rooms and more about everyday glamour. Advances in performance velvets mean the fabric now resists stains and crushing far better than its reputation suggests, while the colour palette has deepened into rich, saturated jewel tones: emerald, forest green, navy and ochre.

A velvet three-seater in a strong colour is the fastest way to give a neutral room a focal point. Keep surrounding tones calm and let the sofa do the talking, or lean into the moment with brass or chrome-legged designs that nod to the Neo Deco mood also trending this year. Our Cello and Lusso ranges cover three-seaters and corners in exactly these shades.

5. Modular layouts that move with you

Fixed three-seaters are no longer the default. Modular sofas made of individual sections that clip together, separate into chairs, or swap a chaise from left to right are surging, and the reason is practical: renters and frequent movers can rebuild the same sofa to fit the next flat instead of selling it at a loss. A modular corner that suits a rectangular living room today can become an L-shape somewhere else tomorrow.

Look for sections with secure but simple connectors, and check whether ottoman pieces can extend the seat into a daybed. The Onda modular corner sofa and the Loop two-seater are built around this flexibility, and modular sofa beds take the idea further by converting individual sections into sleeping space for guests.

6. Low-profile, lounge-low living

Sofas are sitting lower in 2026. Reduced seat heights and shallower overall profiles make ceilings feel taller and rooms feel calmer, and the resulting laid-back posture suits how most households actually use their sofas: stretched out with a laptop or a film, not perched upright. Deep seats and feather-blend cushions complete the sink-in effect.

Low designs pair beautifully with low coffee tables and floor cushions for a cohesive, grounded scheme. If anyone in the household struggles to stand up from deep seating, look for a medium rather than ultra-low height, or add a firmer lumbar cushion to make rising easier.

7. Neo Deco glamour

Named in trend forecasts as the successor to classic Art Deco, Neo Deco is a moodier, sleeker take on twenties glamour: pleated bases, channel stitching, high arms, and metallic detailing in brass or chrome. On sofas it translates into velvet upholstery in deep jewel tones with refined metal feet, a look that feels special without tipping into theme-park territory.

The key to living with Neo Deco is restraint. One statement sofa with metallic detailing is enough; keep walls, curtains and rugs quiet so the glamour reads as intentional. The Gatsby velvet corner sofa and the Deco ochre three-seater were designed squarely for this trend.

How to shop the trends without dating your living room

Trends move faster than sofas wear out, so shop strategically. Put the long-lasting money into shape and comfort: a well-made frame, deep supportive seats and a silhouette you will still like in ten years. Put the trend into fabric and colour, which are easier to refresh with throws, cushions and the occasional re-cover.

Designer tip: pick at most two trends per room. A curved silhouette in a textured weave, or a classic shape in a fashionable fabric, looks considered. Every trend at once looks like a showroom.

And remember that the most popular classic shapes are not going anywhere. The rolled-arm three-seater remains the UK's most-bought traditional silhouette because it suits almost any room, and slimmed-down chesterfields and low Lawson lounges continue to sell steadily alongside the trend-led pieces.

Every sofa at Sofora is delivered free anywhere in the UK on orders over £500 by a two-person team, and you pay only after inspecting it on your doorstep, by cash, card or bank transfer. Each piece also carries a 5-year guarantee, so whichever 2026 trend you choose, it is built to outlast it. Browse the trend-led range, from our curved corner sofas to bouclé armchairs, and find the style your living room has been waiting for.
keyTakeaway: The seven sofa styles defining UK homes in 2026 are curved silhouettes, neater bouclé, jumbo cord, velvet's comeback, modular layouts, low-profile lounging and Neo Deco glamour. The unifying theme is visible comfort: softer shapes, touchable textures and warmer colours replacing cool minimalism. Invest in shape and comfort for longevity, and express trends through fabric and colour.

faqJson.q: What is the most popular sofa style in the UK in 2026?
faqJson.a: Curved sofas are the defining silhouette of 2026, with soft serpentine shapes appearing across three-seaters, corners and armchairs. Classic rolled-arm three-seaters remain the most-bought traditional shape alongside the trend-led designs.

faqJson.q: Is bouclé still fashionable in 2026?
faqJson.a: Yes, but it has matured: the oversized shaggy loops have tightened into neater, more structured weaves that wear better day to day. Cream, ivory and oat remain the most versatile shades.

faqJson.q: Are modular sofas worth it?
faqJson.a: For renters and frequent movers, yes. Sections that rearrange, split into chairs or swap a chaise side let you rebuild the same sofa for a new room instead of selling it at a loss.

faqJson.q: What colours are trending for sofas in 2026?
faqJson.a: Earthy neutrals like oat, sage and natural lead, with dopamine brights such as terracotta and mustard as accents, and deep jewel velvets in emerald, navy and forest green for statement pieces.

title: Bouclé vs Velvet vs Chenille vs Cord: Which Fabric?
metaTitle: Sofa Fabric Guide: Bouclé vs Velvet vs Chenille vs Cord
metaDescription: Bouclé, velvet, chenille or jumbo cord? Our honest sofa fabric guide covers feel, durability, pets, kids, cleaning and cost, with a verdict for every lifestyle.
excerpt: The four fabrics everyone is asking about in 2026, compared honestly on feel, durability, pets, children, cleaning and cost, so you can choose with confidence.
contentHtml:
Choosing a sofa fabric in 2026 means choosing between four textures that dominate every showroom and feed: bouclé, velvet, chenille and jumbo cord. Each looks and feels completely different, and each behaves differently once real life, with its pets, children, snacks and Sunday naps, gets involved. There is no single best fabric, only the best fabric for your household.

This guide compares all four honestly: how they feel, how long they last, how they cope with kids and pets, how hard they are to clean, and what they cost. By the end you will know exactly which one belongs in your living room.

Bouclé: the textured icon

The feel: nubby, looped and unmistakably tactile. Bouclé's curled yarns create a soft, cloud-like surface that reads as quietly luxurious and instantly warms up a room. In 2026 the trend has moved towards tighter, more structured weaves that keep the texture while wearing better than the shaggy versions of a few years ago.

Durability and real life: this is bouclé's weak spot. The looped surface can snag on jewellery, zips and pet claws, so it is not the pick for homes with cats or boisterous toddlers. In a calm living room or snug, however, it holds up well and the broken texture disguises minor marks and creasing.

Cleaning: vacuum with an upholstery attachment regularly to stop dust settling into the loops. Blot spills immediately rather than rubbing. Cost: mid to high; genuine wool-blend bouclés sit at the premium end.

Velvet: the glamorous comeback

The feel: smooth, dense and light-reactive. Velvet's pile shifts shade as you brush it, giving jewel tones like emerald, navy and ochre a depth that flat fabrics cannot match. Modern performance velvets, usually polyester-based, are far more stain-resistant and crush-resistant than traditional cotton velvet.

Durability and real life: better than its reputation, provided you choose a performance velvet. Pet hair sits on the surface rather than weaving in, so it vacuums off easily, though light colours show paw prints. Claws can mark the pile, so it suits households where pets are not allowed on the sofa, or where you are happy to use a throw.

Cleaning: brush weekly with a soft clothes brush to keep the pile even, and deal with spills quickly. Steam can revive flattened areas. Cost: mid-range for polyester velvets, high for cotton and silk blends.

Chenille: the soft all-rounder

The feel: plush and gently fuzzy, like a favourite jumper. Chenille's soft pile feels instantly cosy and comes in an enormous range of colours, from calm neutrals to rich earthy tones. It is the fabric most people picture when they imagine sinking into a sofa.

Durability and real life: this is chenille's superpower. A tight chenille weave is one of the most forgiving family fabrics: it disguises creasing, minor marks and the compression lines that appear on any well-used seat, and it stands up well to children. It is also the safest textured choice for pet owners among the fashionable options.

Cleaning: vacuum regularly and blot spills promptly; many chenilles now come with stain-resistant finishes. Cost: the most budget-friendly of the four, which makes it the value champion.

Jumbo cord: the retro tactile choice

The feel: wide, soft ribs with a relaxed seventies warmth. Jumbo cord is corduroy's chunkier sibling, and the ribbed texture adds visual interest without any pattern to tire of. It feels casual and inviting rather than formal.

Durability and real life: excellent for busy homes. The ribs break up the surface so wear, light soiling and pet hair are far less visible than on flat weaves, and the fabric itself is hard-wearing. It is arguably the most practical fashionable fabric on this list.

Cleaning: vacuum along the ribs and brush occasionally to keep them defined. Cost: mid-range, similar to a good chenille.

The verdict: which fabric for your life?

  • Young children: chenille or jumbo cord. Both forgive spills and rough treatment, and both come with easy-clean finishes.
  • Cats or dogs on the sofa: tight chenille or jumbo cord. Avoid looped bouclé, which claws will catch.
  • Style-first living room: velvet for drama, bouclé for quiet luxury. Keep them in lower-traffic rooms.
  • Tight budget: chenille gives the most comfort per pound.
  • Allergy-prone household: smooth, tight weaves trap less dust than deep piles; vacuum any fabric weekly.

Rub counts: the number worth checking

Fabric durability is measured in rubs on the Martindale test, and it is worth asking for the figure before you buy. As a rough guide, anything above 25,000 rubs suits everyday domestic use, and 30,000 or more is a sensible benchmark for a sofa that will take daily family punishment. Texture helps too: a broken surface like chenille or cord will always disguise wear better than a flat plain weave at the same rub count.

Care cheat sheet

  • Vacuum all upholstery weekly with a soft brush attachment.
  • Blot spills immediately with a clean cloth; never rub.
  • Rotate and plump loose cushions regularly for even wear.
  • Keep sofas out of prolonged direct sunlight to prevent fading.
  • Use throws on the most-sat seats if you have pets.

Whichever fabric you choose, every Sofora sofa is covered by a 5-year guarantee, delivered free anywhere in the UK on orders over £500, and paid for only after you have inspected it on your doorstep. Browse our fabric collections, from bouclé two-seaters to chenille corner sofas, and order swatches of feeling with complete confidence: if it is not right when it arrives, you simply do not pay.
keyTakeaway: Bouclé suits calm, style-led rooms but snags around pets; velvet brings glamour and is easier to live with in modern performance weaves; chenille is the best all-rounder for families; jumbo cord is the most practical fashionable choice for busy homes. Match the fabric to your household, not just your mood board, and look for 30,000+ rubs for daily family use.

faqJson.q: Which sofa fabric is best for homes with pets?
faqJson.a: Tight chenille or jumbo cord. Both resist claws better than looped bouclé and hide pet hair well. Velvet works if pets stay off the sofa, as hair vacuums off the pile easily.

faqJson.q: Is bouclé hard to maintain?
faqJson.a: Not particularly, but it needs regular vacuuming to keep dust out of the loops, and the looped surface can snag on jewellery, zips and pet claws. It suits calmer rooms best.

faqJson.q: What does rub count mean for sofa fabric?
faqJson.a: It is the Martindale test score for abrasion resistance. Above 25,000 rubs suits everyday use, and 30,000 or more is a good benchmark for a sofa facing daily family wear.

faqJson.q: Is velvet practical for a family sofa?
faqJson.a: Modern performance velvets are far more practical than traditional cotton velvet: they resist stains and crushing better. They still show paw prints on light colours, so mid and dark tones are the safer family pick.

title: Curved Sofas: A 2026 Styling Guide
metaTitle: Curved Sofas: How to Style Them in 2026 | Sofora
metaDescription: Curved sofas are 2026's defining shape. Our styling guide covers layouts, pairings, fabrics and small-room tips for a sculptural sofa that looks intentional.
excerpt: The sculptural shape everyone wants this year, styled properly: layouts, pairings, fabrics and small-room tricks for curved sofas.
contentHtml:
Curved sofas are the defining furniture shape of 2026. Serpentine backs, bowed fronts and rounded arms are softening living rooms everywhere, replacing a decade of sharp corners with what designers call soft geometry. But a sculptural sofa is also easier to get wrong than a conventional one: place it badly and it looks awkward rather than artful.

This guide covers everything that makes curved sofas work, from the design logic behind the trend to room layouts, the pieces that pair beautifully with curves, fabric and colour choices, and how to pull the look off in a small room.

Why curves work

Curves do three jobs at once. Visually, they break up the grid of walls, windows and rectangular furniture that makes rooms feel boxy, adding flow and movement. Socially, a gentle arc wraps seating into a conversational shape, so people face each other rather than sitting in a row staring at a screen. Practically, a curved sofa zones an open-plan space: its shape defines a seating area without the need for rugs-as-borders or awkward dividers.

There is also a comfort argument. Rounded arms and continuous backs remove the hard edges you lean against, and most curved designs sit a little lower and deeper than their straight-backed equivalents, encouraging proper lounging.

Layouts that flatter a curved sofa

Float it in open plan. This is the curve's natural habitat. Position the sofa with its back to the dining or kitchen zone and let the arc embrace the seating area. Anchor it with a rug that follows the curve rather than fighting it: round or organic-shaped rugs work best.

Angle it in a square room. A curved corner sofa placed across a corner, rather than pushed hard into it, softens a boxy room and creates useful space behind for a floor lamp or a tall plant. Our Arco curved corner sofa was designed for exactly this placement.

Against the wall, with breathing room. If floating is not an option, pull the sofa a hand's width off the wall. The shadow gap emphasises the sculptural back instead of flattening it, and it makes the whole piece look deliberately placed.

What to pair it with

  • Round coffee tables: echo the curve rather than contrasting it. A round or oval table sits naturally inside the arc.
  • An arc floor lamp: the classic partner, its sweep mirroring the sofa's line while giving you proper reading light.
  • Curved armchairs: one is enough. A tub chair such as the Elsie in a complementary fabric extends the language without overdoing it.
  • Textured rugs: bouclé, high-pile wool or jute rugs underfoot reinforce the softness. Avoid harsh geometric patterns that fight the shape.
  • Soft lighting: globe pendants, paper lanterns and curved shades keep the mood consistent.

Fabrics and colours that suit curves

Texture is the curve's best friend. Bouclé's nubby surface emphasises every contour and is the definitive curved-sofa fabric of 2026, which is why our Juno curved three-seater pairs the two. Velvet runs a close second: its light-reactive pile makes arcs glow, especially in jewel tones like emerald or navy. Jumbo cord adds a relaxed, retro warmth that stops sculptural shapes feeling pretentious.

On colour, curves forgive boldness. A terracotta or ochre curve becomes a joyful focal point in a neutral room, while ivory and oat curves disappear elegantly into calm schemes. If your walls are already busy, keep the sofa quiet and let the shape do the talking.

Curved sofas in small rooms

Small rooms can absolutely take a curve; in fact, rounded shapes often fit better than expected because there are no sharp corners jutting into walkways. Choose a compact design like a 150–160cm curved two-seater rather than a full corner, keep the profile low so sightlines stay open, and let one curve be the star: a curved sofa plus a round rug is plenty in a snug.

Measure the arc's widest points, not just the headline width, and check the footprint against your floor plan with masking tape before ordering. Curves are less forgiving of tight squeezes than straight sofas.

Curved sofas beyond the living room

Curves are not confined to the main living room. A compact curved two-seater makes a wonderful bedroom reading corner, softening a space that is otherwise all straight wardrobe lines. In a home office, a small curved loveseat creates a welcoming spot for calls that a desk chair never could. Even hallways and landings can take a petite curved bench, turning dead space into somewhere to pause. Wherever a conventional sofa would feel blocky or imposing, a curve slips in gracefully.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Too many curves: a curved sofa, curved chairs, a round rug and an arc lamp can tip into theme. Two curved elements per room is the sweet spot.
  • Pushing it flat against the wall: hides the very shape you paid for. Give it breathing room.
  • Pairing with harsh geometry: chevron rugs and angular side tables argue with the sofa. Keep lines soft.
  • Ignoring the back: curved sofas are often seen from behind in open plan, so choose a design with a finished, attractive back.

Stylist's rule of thumb: if you can trace one continuous flowing line from your sofa through your rug to your lighting, the room will feel calm. Curves want company, just not competition.

Ready to bring soft geometry home? Sofora's curved range spans compact two-seaters to sweeping five-seat corners in bouclé, velvet and cord. Every order over £500 includes free UK delivery by a two-person team, you pay only after inspecting your sofa on the doorstep, and each piece carries a 5-year guarantee. A sculptural sofa is a confident choice; buying it should feel like a safe one.
keyTakeaway: Curved sofas are 2026's defining shape because they soften boxy rooms, encourage conversation and zone open-plan spaces. Style them by floating or angling the placement, pairing with round tables and soft lighting, choosing textured fabrics like bouclé or velvet, and limiting curves to two elements per room. Compact curved two-seaters work well even in small rooms.

faqJson.q: Do curved sofas work in small living rooms?
faqJson.a: Yes. Rounded shapes have no sharp corners jutting into walkways, and a compact 150–160cm curved two-seater with a low profile suits a snug well. Measure the arc's widest points before ordering.

faqJson.q: What coffee table goes with a curved sofa?
faqJson.a: A round or oval coffee table echoes the curve and sits naturally inside the arc. Avoid harsh rectangular or angular tables that fight the sofa's lines.

faqJson.q: What fabric is best for a curved sofa?
faqJson.a: Bouclé is the definitive pairing: its texture emphasises every contour. Velvet is a close second for a glamorous look, and jumbo cord adds relaxed retro warmth.

faqJson.q: Where should you place a curved sofa?
faqJson.a: Float it in open-plan spaces with its back to the dining or kitchen zone, or angle a curved corner across a room corner. Against a wall, pull it a hand's width out so the sculptural back shows.

title: How to Measure for a New Sofa (UK Guide)
metaTitle: How to Measure for a Sofa: Doorways, Stairs & Rooms
metaDescription: Measure your room, doorways, stairs and delivery route before you buy. Our UK guide gives you the key steps, standard door widths and a delivery-day checklist.
excerpt: The number one cause of sofa delivery problems is skipping the tape measure. Here is the exact UK measuring routine, from room footprint to stairwell turns.
contentHtml:
More sofa deliveries go wrong because of measurements than for any other reason. The sofa is perfect, the room is ready, and then it will not fit through the front door, around the stairwell turn, or into the space you imagined. Every one of these problems is preventable with a tape measure and twenty minutes.

This UK guide walks you through the three measurements that matter: your room's footprint, your doorways and access points, and the full delivery route. Do all three before you order and delivery day becomes the easy part.

What you will need

  • A tape measure (a 5m one is ideal)
  • Masking tape or newspaper for outlining footprints
  • A notepad or your phone for recording numbers
  • The sofa's full dimensions: width, depth and height, plus diagonal depth if the retailer provides it

Step 1: map your room

Measure the length and width of the room, then mark out the sofa's footprint on the floor with masking tape using its width and depth. This simple trick is the single most useful thing you can do: it shows you instantly whether the sofa overwhelms the space, blocks a radiator, or crowds a walkway.

Live with the outline for a day. Walk your normal routes around it, open nearby doors and drawers, and check you can still reach windows and sockets comfortably. As a rough guide, you want enough space to walk past the sofa without turning sideways, and at least enough clearance to pull out any sofa-bed mechanism or recliner footrest fully. If the tape outline feels tight, it will feel tighter with the real thing.

Also note the room's fixed features: radiators, plug sockets, TV position and window heights. A high-backed sofa in front of a low windowsill can block light and look wrong from outside.

Step 2: measure your doorways

This is where most problems start. Measure every doorway the sofa must pass through, and measure the narrowest point, which is usually the door frame itself rather than the open door. Most UK internal doors are around 76cm wide, and that is often tighter than people expect. External doors are typically wider, around 90cm, but check yours rather than assuming.

Record three numbers per doorway: the width at the narrowest point, the height, and the diagonal. The diagonal matters because sofas are rarely carried straight through: tilting a sofa onto its end and angling it through is standard practice, and the diagonal clearance decides whether that manoeuvre works. If a door can be lifted off its hinges, note that too; it commonly buys you an extra few centimetres.

Compare the narrowest doorway against the sofa's height and diagonal depth. If the numbers are close, that is your cue to double-check rather than hope.

Step 3: hallways, stairs and tight turns

Doorways get the attention, but stairwells cause the most failed deliveries. Measure the width of your staircase, the height of the ceiling above the stairs, and any turns or landings. On a turn, the critical measurement is the diagonal space available: the delivery team needs room to pivot a long object around the corner.

Hallways matter as well. Measure their width and note anything that narrows them: radiators, coat hooks, console tables, low ceilings. Anything that can be temporarily moved should be, and anything that cannot needs to be in your measurements.

For flats, do not forget the communal areas: the building's front door, corridors, and especially the lift. Measure the lift's internal width, depth and door opening. A surprising number of sofas fit the flat but not the lift.

Step 4: the delivery route checklist

  1. Walk the entire route from the kerb to the sofa's final position, exactly as the delivery team will.
  2. Measure every doorway, hallway, stair turn and lift on that route at its narrowest point.
  3. Note low ceilings, tight turns, radiators and fixed furniture.
  4. Identify what can be moved on the day and what cannot.
  5. Check whether doors can come off their hinges for extra clearance.
  6. Confirm the final position: footprint taped out, walkways clear, sockets reachable.
  7. Keep your measurements somewhere you can find them when you order.

Extra clearance for sofa beds and recliners

Mechanisms need space to move. A sofa bed needs its full sleeping length clear in front of it, typically around 140cm wide by 190cm long for a double, plus room to stand beside it while pulling it out. Recliners need clearance behind for the backrest to tilt and in front for the footrest. Tape these extended footprints on the floor too; a sofa that fits closed but not open is a common disappointment.

What if it will not fit?

Do not force it. If your measurements show a genuinely tight squeeze, consider a modular sofa: individual sections are far easier to carry through narrow Victorian terraces and up winding stairs than one rigid frame, and they clip together in the room. Removable legs can also buy crucial centimetres. And if the numbers simply do not work, choosing a slightly smaller model beats a failed delivery every time.

Delivery teams can work wonders with angles and tilts, but they cannot bend physics. When in doubt, send your measurements to the retailer before ordering and ask for an honest opinion.

At Sofora, delivery is handled by a two-person team who will carry your sofa to the room of your choice, and because you pay only after inspecting it on your doorstep, there is no financial risk if something unexpected happens on the day. Orders over £500 include free UK delivery, and every sofa carries a 5-year guarantee. Measure twice, order once, and enjoy the easy part.
keyTakeaway: Prevent delivery problems by measuring three things before ordering: the room footprint (tape it out on the floor), every doorway at its narrowest point (most UK internal doors are around 76cm), and the full delivery route including stairs, turns and lifts. Sofa beds and recliners need their extended footprints measured too. If access is tight, modular sofas are far easier to deliver.

faqJson.q: What is the standard UK internal door width?
faqJson.a: Most UK internal doors are around 76cm wide, measured at the narrowest point of the frame. External doors are typically around 90cm, but always measure your own rather than assuming.

faqJson.q: How do I check if a sofa will fit through my door?
faqJson.a: Measure the doorway's width, height and diagonal at the narrowest point, and compare against the sofa's height and diagonal depth. Remember doors can often be lifted off hinges for a few extra centimetres.

faqJson.q: How much space should I leave around a sofa?
faqJson.a: Tape the sofa's footprint on the floor and check you can walk your normal routes without squeezing past. Sofa beds and recliners need their fully extended footprints clear as well.

faqJson.q: Will a sofa fit up my stairs?
faqJson.a: Measure the stair width, the ceiling height above the stairs, and the diagonal space at any turn or landing, since the delivery team must pivot the sofa around corners. For flats, measure the lift's internal dimensions too.

title: Cash on Delivery Sofas: How It Works
metaTitle: Cash on Delivery Sofas: How It Works | Sofora
metaDescription: Order a sofa online with zero upfront payment. Here's how Sofora's cash-on-delivery model works, from phone confirmation to paying the driver after inspection.
excerpt: Order online, pay nothing upfront, and hand over payment only after inspecting your sofa on the doorstep. How cash-on-delivery sofa shopping works, step by step.
contentHtml:
Buying a sofa online usually means paying hundreds of pounds upfront for something you have never sat on, then hoping the delivery matches the photos. Cash on delivery turns that around: you order online, pay nothing in advance, and hand over payment only after the sofa is in your home and you have inspected it. If it is not right, you do not pay.

This is exactly how Sofora works, and it is why a growing number of UK shoppers now refuse to buy big-ticket furniture any other way. Here is the process step by step, why shoppers love it, and how it compares to paying upfront or taking finance.

How Sofora's cash on delivery works

  1. Order online. Choose your sofa and check out on the website with your name, address and phone number. No card details, no deposit, no payment of any kind at this stage.
  2. We confirm by phone. A member of the Sofora team calls you to confirm your order, check the details, and agree a delivery slot that suits you. This call also lets us double-check access, so there are no surprises on the day.
  3. Two-person delivery. On delivery day, a two-person team brings your sofa to your home and carries it to the room of your choice. Delivery is free anywhere in the UK on orders over £500.
  4. Inspect before you pay. This is the heart of the model. Check the fabric, the colour, the stitching, the comfort, sit on it, look it over properly. Take your time; the team expects it.
  5. Pay the driver. Happy with everything? Pay there and then by cash, debit or credit card, or bank transfer, whichever suits you. Only at this point does any money change hands.

Why UK shoppers love it

No paying for something unseen. The fundamental worry with online furniture is the gap between photos and reality. Cash on delivery closes that gap completely: the product is in front of you before a single pound leaves your account.

No card fraud risk. You never enter card details on a website, so there is nothing to be skimmed, breached or misused. For shoppers wary of online payment fraud, that alone is decisive.

Budget control. The money stays in your account until delivery day, earning interest or simply available for anything else life throws at you in the meantime. There is no deposit tied up for weeks while you wait.

No finance applications. No credit checks, no interest, no monthly payments, no fine print. You pay once, in full, when you are holding the goods.

Trust for big purchases. A sofa is one of the largest single purchases most households make in a year. Being able to verify it first transforms the experience from a leap of faith into a straightforward transaction.

Cash on delivery vs paying upfront vs finance

Paying upfront by card does give you credit-card purchase protection, but it still means your money is gone before the goods arrive, and resolving problems means chasing refunds. Finance spreads the cost but adds interest, credit checks and contractual commitment before you have even seen the product.

Cash on delivery inverts the risk entirely: the retailer's money is tied up, not yours. The seller has every incentive to get the product and the delivery right first time, because payment depends on your satisfaction at the door. For the shopper, it is the lowest-risk way to buy furniture online.

What you can pay with

Despite the name, cash on delivery at Sofora is not cash-only. When the delivery team arrives, you can pay by cash, by debit or credit card using the driver's card machine, or by bank transfer on the spot. Choose whichever you are comfortable with; the price is the same.

Delivery day: what to expect

Make sure someone is home for the agreed slot and that the delivery route is clear: the measuring guide on our blog walks through doorways, stairs and access if you want to prepare. The team will carry the sofa to your chosen room, and packaging is taken care of. Then comes the inspection: check the colour in your own light, sit in your usual spots, open any sofa-bed or recliner mechanisms, and look over the stitching and legs.

Take the inspection seriously. Sit where you will actually sit, in daylight if possible. A good delivery team would rather wait five minutes than come back.

Who cash on delivery suits best

Cash on delivery particularly suits first-time online furniture buyers who have never bought a big-ticket item without seeing it, anyone who has been burnt by a disappointing delivery in the past, and shoppers who simply prefer to keep their finances simple: no credit agreements, no deposits held for weeks, no refund chases. It also suits the cautious gift-buyer furnishing a relative's home from a distance, since the recipient can inspect the sofa on arrival and you only pay when they are happy.

Is there a catch?

The honest answer: very little. You need to be home for the delivery slot, and the team needs reasonable access, which is true of any furniture delivery. There is no deposit, no obligation, and no penalty if you inspect the sofa and decide it is not for you. That is the entire point of the model.

Every Sofora sofa also carries a 5-year guarantee, so the confidence does not end at the doorstep. Order online today with nothing to pay upfront, get free UK delivery on orders over £500, inspect your sofa in your own home, and pay only when you love it. That is furniture shopping the way it should be.

faqJson.q: How does cash on delivery work for sofas?
faqJson.a: You order online with no payment, the retailer confirms by phone and delivers, you inspect the sofa in your home, and only then do you pay the driver by cash, card or bank transfer.

faqJson.q: Do I pay a deposit when ordering a sofa on cash on delivery?
faqJson.a: No. With Sofora's model there is no deposit and no card details taken at checkout. The first and only payment happens on delivery day after your inspection.

faqJson.q: What if I don't like the sofa when it arrives?
faqJson.a: Then you don't pay. The inspection before payment is the core of cash on delivery: if the sofa isn't right, no money changes hands.

faqJson.q: Is delivery free with cash on delivery sofas?
faqJson.a: At Sofora, delivery anywhere in the UK is free on orders over £500, carried out by a two-person team who bring the sofa to your room of choice.
